title: Short Stuff: Mexican Jumping Beans
summary: Short Stuff episode on Mexican jumping beans. The hosts explain that the jumping "beans" are seed pods from the yerba de flecha (Sebastiania pavoniana) shrub, native to rocky slopes in Sonora and Chihuahua, Mexico. Early US sightings date to the 1920s in San Francisco, and a twelve-year-old Joaquin Hernandez of Alamos, Sonora, later marketed them as a novelty and became known as the jumping bean king. Entomologists found that a live jumping bean moth larva inside the pod causes the movement: the larva eats the seed from the inside and its silk-attached cocoon moves the pod, similar to a whip's crack. The hosts describe heat making the pods move as a possible adaptation for seeking shade, warn that heating them can kill the larva, and mention keeping them as pets by keeping them cool and misted.
topics: keeping Mexican jumping beans as pets

segments.title: Intro and childhood memories of Mexican jumping beans
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode, note Jerry is away, and discuss whether they knew about Mexican jumping beans as kids and whether they had seen them in person.

segments.title: What the jumping beans are and the yerba de flecha plant
segments.summary: The hosts explain the jumping beans are seed pods, not beans, from the yerba de flecha shrub, whose name means herb of the arrow, and describe its leaves and range in Sonora and Chihuahua.

segments.title: Arrival in the United States in the 1920s
segments.summary: The beans first reached the States in San Francisco in the 1920s, when a Chronicle article described the seeds as delighting people of all ages.

segments.title: Joaquin Hernandez, the jumping bean king
segments.summary: Joaquin Hernandez, who was twelve in the 1940s, saw the commercial potential of the seeds, marketed them to joke shops, and became known as the jumping bean king; Alamos, Sonora is the jumping bean capital.

segments.title: The moth larva that makes the beans jump
segments.summary: Early theories included static charge and trapped gas before entomologists found a live moth larva inside each pod. The larva eats the seed from the inside and its silk cocoon, attached to the pod walls, moves the pod like a whip crack.

segments.title: Heat, shade-seeking, and caring for the beans
segments.summary: Heat makes the pods move, possibly an adaptation to seek shade, but heating them can kill the larva. The hosts discuss keeping them as pets by keeping them cool and misted, citing jbean.com.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the episode and sign off with the standard credits.
